Matched RecHarness Amazon task: four datasets Movies_and_TV,
Industrial_and_Scientific, Electronics, CDs_and_Vinyl, macro-average validation
HR@10. Start from RecHarness sasrec_perdataset. Preprocessing seed=0 and training
seed=42, exactly as run2.sh. The host executes your train.py and then independently
evaluates working/predict.py using the pinned RecHarness benchmark (200 validation
users/category, 99 unique negative candidates, evaluation seed=42). Test labels and
test metrics are unavailable during search. Retain all four categories and dataset
routing. DATA_DIR must remain os.environ['GAGC_DATA_DIR']; write artifacts beneath
your trial directory, as the baseline does. Training may change model architecture,
loss, optimizer, sampling and hyperparameters, as in RecHarness. Do not alter input
splits, invent metrics, read hidden test files, fetch extra datasets/pretrained weights,
or change the host evaluator. Changes to inference must also update the predictor
writer so working/predict.py loads the trained architecture. Keep execution single-GPU;
the host provides four concurrent trial slots and 64 CPU cores. No shell actions,
filesystem inspection, or training tools are needed in the LLM call: return code.
All training, diagnostics, debugging and failed trials consume the method's shared
43,200 GPU-second search budget. LLM time and final held-out inference are recorded
separately, matching run2.sh's separate final-evaluation step.
The original RecHarness tools layer sets SASREC_EPOCHS=200 (overriding the template's
standalone default of 300); this same environment default applies here.

METHOD: self_evolverec

Diagnostic task adapter: diagnosis_tools.py must retain class DiagnosisProbe(view, device)
and method run_full_diagnosis(train_loader), returning metrics and metric_definitions.
It must also retain callable diagnosis_interpreter_prompt(raw_diagnosis), returning
the diagnostic interpretation prompt using measured metrics and their definitions.
view.model is the actual trained nn.Module. view.item_emb, log2feats(sequence),
predict_score(features, items), user_train, meta_data, review_data implement the
initial SASRec compatibility contract. Adapt probes when changing the architecture.
train_loader yields (None, sequence, positive, negative), tensors of shape B x L.
Only public interaction histories, item titles, descriptions and timestamps are available.
Review ratings/text, item ratings/categories/prices/stores are NOT available in this
shared RecHarness task. Never invent them. Simulator diversity/conformity traits are
explicitly unobserved. Twenty real training users (five/category) receive full-catalog
unseen-item recommendations, as the native simulator requires. Selection uses the
common macro validation HR@10, replacing the native HR@5/NDCG@5 combined score.

NATIVE ROLE: Reflection Agent

You are an expert research assistant. You will receive a research report (in Markdown) and a newly proposed idea for that report's research problem. Your job is to identify any gaps or issues—such as missing details, logical flaws, or questionable evaluations of novelty, impact, or implementation difficulty.  

- If the report and idea contain all necessary information, do not generate any follow-up questions.  
- If you detect a knowledge gap or something that needs deeper exploration, generate one or more self-contained follow-up queries. Each query must include enough context so that a web search could answer it, For each query, give a short note explaining why you use the query and what you hope it will reveal.
- Focus on technical details, implementation specifics, and any emerging methods or references that were overlooked.  
- Use clear, direct language and avoid unnecessary jargon.

 ## Search results
Evidence supports testing more negatives before changing SASRec’s architecture. [gSASRec (IJCAI 2024)](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2024/939) identifies overconfidence from sampled BCE and introduces generalized BCE; its [extended abstract](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2024/0939.pdf) recommends 128–256 negatives and calibration parameter t=0.75, balancing effectiveness against computation. These are useful experimental starting points, not established optima for this benchmark. Compare single-negative BCE, multi-negative BCE/gBCE, and sampled-softmax cross-entropy under comparable GPU budgets; increasing negative count alone does not correct sampling bias.

Hardness needs scheduling and false-negative controls. [R²NS (WWW 2026)](https://renzhaochun.github.io/assets/pdf/WWW_2026_Camera_Ready.pdf) combines uniform-sampling warm-up, global candidate recall, and progressively harder stochastic top-M selection; it reports that introducing hard negatives too early can underperform uniform sampling. [CATS (SIGIR 2026)](https://iris.uniroma1.it/handle/11573/1775773) adaptively samples across item clusters while reducing sampling from the positive item’s own cluster, motivated by false-negative risk. Practical inference: first test uniform multi-negative objectives; then mix uniform and moderately hard negatives after warm-up, excluding known training positives and avoiding deterministic hardest-only selection. Use learned interaction embeddings for optional similarity controls; similarity does not establish a true false negative. Select by the prescribed four-category macro validation HR@10 and inspect Electronics separately. Larger diagnostic margins or published gains on other datasets do not establish improvement under this evaluator.

---

Recent work supports combining individual sequences with global item transitions. [TGCL4SR (AAAI 2024)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/28789) builds a temporal item-transition graph, combines graph convolution with a time-aware Transformer, and adds contrastive objectives. [LS4SRec (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3723173) uses a weighted global transition graph to supply collaborative signals for sparse sequences while separating long- and short-term interests. For explicit relation types, [KGSCL (2025)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S089360802500070X) distinguishes substitution and complementarity through Amazon metadata relationships, using substitution for replacement augmentation and complementarity for insertion. Those relationship annotations are unavailable in this task; its reported gains do not establish that histories and text alone recover the same semantics.

A feasible adaptation—an inference from these methods—is SASRec plus separate directed-transition and lexical-similarity channels, with a learned gate controlling their contributions. Build transitions exclusively from training histories; encode titles/descriptions using TF-IDF or randomly initialized pooled token embeddings trained with next-item prediction. Treat channels as behavioral succession and textual similarity: neither provides verified complement/substitute labels. Much recent text-based evidence depends on external pretrained representations; [WhitenRec (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.10602), for example, explicitly uses pretrained text embeddings, so its gains cannot justify a scratch-trained encoder. The search found no directly verified 2024–2026 result establishing the complete proposed combination under these restrictions. Test transition-only, text-only, and gated combinations against SASRec using the pinned macro validation HR@10, with history-length breakdowns to assess sparse-user benefits.

---

Recent work supports separating stable preferences from changing intent. [Teddy (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ipm.2023.103619) adaptively partitions history into dominant trends and scattered interests, using temporal convolutions and pooled MLP features respectively. [IDCLRec (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.07096) extracts consistent interests through causal cross-attention, models residual behavior as dynamic intent, and adds item-aware contrastive supervision. Its criticism of arbitrary fixed intent counts is relevant: multiple representation heads alone do not establish meaningful disentanglement.

Temporal modeling offers a complementary axis. [HyperHawkes](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=t0q7KbmB7o) combines clustered latent intents, temporal processes for recurring consumption, and attention mixtures for immediate interests. [DSRec (September 2026 preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21548) separates historical preferences from local intent, using distinct state-space encoders and inter-click intervals to modulate the short-term branch. These approaches motivate distinguishing sequence position, elapsed time, and intent recurrence rather than assuming uniform recency decay; their reported benchmark improvements do not establish gains under this task’s evaluator.

Practical inference for the constrained SASRec search: retain the sequence encoder, add a pooled historical-interest branch and a recent-window branch, then learn a gate conditioned on observed history and timestamp gaps. A few latent interest queries could preserve alternative purposes, with a modest diversity penalty tested against representation collapse. Purchase saturation remains a hypothesis requiring validation: recurring interest supports renewed demand, while recent consumption may suppress it. ## Starting Research Idea
SASRec predicts the next item using causal self-attention over a user's interaction history. Item and positional embeddings pass through attention and feed-forward blocks; the resulting representation scores candidate items by dot product. Attention can emphasize recent interactions or longer-range dependencies. Source: [Self-Attentive Sequential Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/html/1808.09781v1).
